analysis.one_liner: Raises the government's proof bar and ends agencies keeping seized-cash proceeds.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan civil asset forfeiture reform bill never received a committee vote or floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fifth Amendment Integrity Restoration Act would have changed federal civil asset forfeiture, the process by which the government takes cash, cars, and other property from people who often have not been charged with a crime. It would have required the government to prove its case by 'clear and convincing evidence' instead of the much lower 'preponderance' standard, guaranteed a lawyer for property owners who cannot afford one, and given owners a fast hearing to get seized money back unless the government shows probable cause. It also would have ended 'equitable sharing,' the practice of routing forfeiture proceeds to law enforcement agencies' own accounts, and sent the money to the Treasury's general fund instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Property owners targeted by federal civil forfeiture, especially people whose cash is seized on suspicion of 'structuring' bank deposits to avoid reporting rules. They would get counsel regardless of ability to pay, a higher burden of proof against the government, a fast probable-cause hearing for seized money, and courts weighing whether taking the property is disproportionate to the offense.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the government's burden of proof in civil forfeiture cases from a preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence, and requires a substantial connection between the property and the offense [S2][S3].
Guarantees counsel for an indigent property owner regardless of whether the owner requests counsel, under the CRS summary of the bill [S2].

Adds 'knowingly' to the structuring offense and requires a probable-cause hearing within 14 days of notice for seized money, with the property returned unless the government shows probable cause [S2][S3].
Ends equitable sharing and directs forfeiture proceeds to the Treasury general fund instead of the Department of Justice Assets Forfeiture Fund [S2][S3].
Directs courts to consider factors including the seriousness of the offense, the property's value, and hardship to the owner when deciding whether a forfeiture is disproportionate [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies, which would lose the dedicated forfeiture and equitable-sharing revenue they use to fund operations, and would face a higher bar to keep seized property. Prosecutors would also bear more evidentiary work in forfeiture cases.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and local law enforcement agencies

drawbacks.text: Law enforcement argues that forfeiture is a tool against drug trafficking organizations and money laundering, and that a higher evidentiary standard and restored funds to the Treasury would weaken that tool; the bill removes dedicated forfeiture revenue that agencies have relied on to fund equipment and operations [S2].

The clear-and-convincing standard and the knowing-intent requirement for structuring cases would make it harder for the government to win forfeiture even in some legitimate cases, potentially returning money derived from crime to its holders [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for property owners address a well-documented problem: people can lose cash and property without ever being charged, and getting it back is costly and slow. The costs fall mainly on law enforcement budgets and on the government's ability to win borderline cases, which is partly the point of the reform. The bill is a targeted fix rather than abolition of forfeiture, so the trade-off favors the property-owner protections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in committee. It was referred to four committees and three subcommittees, and no committee ever voted on it before the 117th Congress ended, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg introduced the bill on April 26, 2021, joined by five original cosponsors from both parties: Reps. Raskin, McClintock, Cardenas, Rush, and Armstrong [S3].
The bill was referred to four committees on the day it was introduced: Judiciary, plus Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Financial Services [S5].
It was then referred to the Subcommittees on Trade, Health, and Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security [S5].
The bill accumulated 36 cosponsors, 16 Democrats and 20 Republicans [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies that rely on forfeiture and equitable-sharing proceeds are better off, since nothing changed: the government keeps the existing lower evidentiary standard and its dedicated forfeiture funds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies keeping forfeiture proceeds

for.name: Reps. Jamie Raskin, Tom McClintock, Tony Cardenas, Bobby Rush, and Kelly Armstrong
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill sponsors from both parties.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of primary referral; chaired by Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the 117th Congress; no committee vote was ever taken.

against.name: Speaker of the House referral structure
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to four committees at once, which split jurisdiction and made passage harder, as the action history shows.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 36 cosponsors split almost evenly between parties (16 Democrats, 20 Republicans), with original sponsors from both parties; it died without any vote rather than being defeated on partisan lines [S4][S3].

industries.industry: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies currently keep forfeiture proceeds, including through equitable sharing with local police, funding their own operations. The bill would send that money to the Treasury general fund and raise the bar for keeping seized property, directly cutting a revenue stream that comes from private citizens' assets.

industries.industry: Department of Justice Assets Forfeiture Fund
industries.note: The bill strips the fund's dedicated deposits and its equitable-sharing authority, ending the practice of agencies funding themselves from seized property.
